outputs.L1: A control device for a fuel cell system includes an anode gas circulation flow rate control unit configured to control an anode gas circulation flow rate based on a wet/dry state of an electrolyte membrane detected by a wet/dry state detecting unit, and a priority setting unit configured to set priority levels of normal manipulation for a plurality of physical quantities manipulated by a wet/dry state control unit. The anode gas circulation flow rate control unit includes an anode gas circulation flow rate limiting unit configured to limit a rate of change per unit time of the anode gas circulation flow rate during a transient operation for changing the wet/dry state of the electrolyte membrane, and a control quantity compensating unit configured to, when the rate of change is limited, compensate for an insufficiency in a control quantity of the wet/dry state caused by the limitation of the anode gas circulation flow rate. The compensation is carried out by manipulating a physical quantity having a lower priority level of normal manipulation than the priority level of normal manipulation of the anode gas circulation flow rate set by the priority setting unit.
outputs.L2: A fuel cell system control apparatus is provided with an anode gas circulation flow-rate controller that regulates the circulation rate of the anode gas according to the dry or wet condition of the electrolyte membrane, as identified by a wet/dry condition detector. The apparatus also includes a priority setter that assigns priority rankings for ordinary control operations to multiple physical parameters adjusted by the wet/dry condition controller. The anode gas circulation flow-rate controller has a limiting section that restricts the amount by which the anode gas circulation flow rate may change per unit time during transient operation performed to alter the electrolyte membrane’s wet/dry condition. It also has a control-amount compensation section that, when such a rate-of-change restriction is applied, makes up for any shortage in the wet/dry condition control amount caused by the restriction on the anode gas circulation flow rate. This compensation is performed by adjusting a physical parameter whose ordinary-control priority is lower than the ordinary-control priority assigned to the anode gas circulation flow rate by the priority setter.
outputs.L3:
The fuel cell system includes a control device that manages the wet or dry state of the electrolyte membrane by regulating the circulation flow rate of anode gas. The electrolyte membrane must be maintained within an appropriate moisture range in order to ensure stable power generation performance and prevent degradation. If the membrane becomes too dry, proton conductivity may decrease, reducing fuel cell output. Conversely, if the membrane becomes excessively wet, flooding may occur, interfering with gas diffusion and lowering efficiency. Therefore, the control device detects or estimates the wet/dry state of the electrolyte membrane and adjusts the anode gas circulation flow rate accordingly.

The system also includes a priority setting unit that assigns priority levels to the normal manipulation of multiple physical quantities used for managing the membrane wet/dry state. These physical quantities may include, for example, the anode gas circulation flow rate, cathode gas flow rate, humidification amount, coolant temperature, pressure, or other operating parameters that influence the moisture balance of the membrane. Under normal conditions, the control device selects and manipulates these quantities according to their assigned priority levels so that membrane moisture can be controlled efficiently and reliably.

An anode gas circulation flow rate control unit is provided to control the rate at which anode gas is circulated through the fuel cell system. During transient operation, such as rapid load changes or sudden shifts in operating conditions, the control unit limits the rate of change of the anode gas circulation flow rate. This limitation prevents abrupt changes in gas flow that could destabilize system operation, cause pressure fluctuations, reduce durability of components, or negatively affect fuel cell performance.

However, when the change in the anode gas circulation flow rate is limited, the desired wet/dry state control of the electrolyte membrane may not be fully achieved by anode gas circulation control alone. To address this, the system includes a control quantity compensating unit. When the anode gas circulation flow rate cannot be changed sufficiently or quickly enough, this compensating unit supplements the wet/dry state control by adjusting another controllable physical quantity.

The compensation is carried out by manipulating a physical quantity that has a lower priority for normal wet/dry state management than the anode gas circulation flow rate. In other words, the anode gas circulation flow rate remains the preferred control parameter during ordinary operation, but when its rate of change is restricted, a lower-priority control parameter is temporarily used to compensate for the insufficient control effect. This enables the fuel cell system to maintain the electrolyte membrane in an appropriate moisture condition even during transient operation, while also avoiding excessive or abrupt changes in the anode gas circulation flow rate.
outputs.L4:
A fuel cell system control device is configured to manage the wet/dry state of an electrolyte membrane in a fuel cell stack by controlling the operating conditions of the fuel cell system. In particular, the control device controls an anode gas circulation flow rate, which is the flow rate of anode gas recirculated through the anode side of the fuel cell stack. By adjusting this circulation flow rate, the device can influence the amount of water retained in or removed from the electrolyte membrane, thereby helping to prevent both excessive drying and excessive flooding of the membrane.

The control device is also configured to use a plurality of manipulable physical quantities that affect the wet/dry state of the electrolyte membrane. These physical quantities may include, for example, the anode gas circulation flow rate, cathode gas flow rate, cathode pressure, anode pressure, coolant temperature, stack operating temperature, generated current, or other controllable operating parameters of the fuel cell system. Since these physical quantities may have different levels of influence on membrane humidity and different effects on system stability, response, efficiency, and durability, the control device assigns priority levels to them. A higher-priority physical quantity is used preferentially to control the membrane state, while lower-priority physical quantities are used as supplementary control means when necessary.

During steady operation, the control device may control the wet/dry state of the electrolyte membrane mainly by adjusting the anode gas circulation flow rate according to a target membrane state. For example, when the electrolyte membrane tends to become dry, the control device may increase or otherwise modify the anode gas circulation flow in a manner that promotes water retention or redistribution. When the membrane tends to become excessively wet, the control device may adjust the circulation flow rate to enhance water removal and suppress flooding. In this way, the membrane can be maintained within an appropriate humidity range, improving power generation performance and durability.

During transient operation, however, such as rapid acceleration, rapid deceleration, sudden load change, start-up, or other operating condition changes, an abrupt change in anode gas circulation flow rate may adversely affect the stability of the fuel cell system. For instance, a sudden increase or decrease in circulation flow may disturb gas pressure, gas concentration, water distribution, or pump operation, and may result in reduced controllability, increased noise, decreased efficiency, or degradation of fuel cell performance. Therefore, the control device limits the rate of change or the amount of change of the anode gas circulation flow rate during such transient operation.

When the anode gas circulation flow rate is limited in this manner, the desired control effect on the electrolyte membrane wet/dry state may not be fully achieved by the anode gas circulation flow rate alone. To address this, the control device compensates for the resulting control shortfall by using one or more lower-priority manipulable physical quantities. For example, if the anode gas circulation flow rate cannot be increased quickly enough to achieve the target membrane humidity, the control device may adjust the cathode gas flow rate, cathode pressure, stack temperature, coolant flow, generated current, or another controllable parameter to supplement the membrane-state control. These lower-priority physical quantities are selected and adjusted according to their assigned priority levels, their effectiveness in correcting the wet/dry state, and their influence on overall system operation.

As a result, the fuel cell system control device can continue to control the wet/dry state of the electrolyte membrane with high accuracy even when the primary control parameter, namely the anode gas circulation flow rate, cannot be changed rapidly. At the same time, because sudden changes in anode gas circulation are suppressed, the system can avoid instability and maintain smooth operation during transient conditions. This coordinated control improves the balance between membrane humidity management, power generation stability, system responsiveness, and component durability.

Accordingly, the control device enables reliable wet/dry state control of the electrolyte membrane while preventing excessive operational disturbances in the fuel cell system. By assigning priority levels to multiple manipulable physical quantities and using lower-priority quantities to compensate when higher-priority control is restricted, the device achieves robust membrane-state management under both steady and transient operating conditions.
outputs.L5:
A control device is an important component used to manage, regulate, and monitor the operation of machines, systems, or electronic equipment. It allows users to start, stop, adjust, or automate different functions depending on the needs of the application. Control devices can be simple, such as switches, buttons, and remote controls, or more advanced, such as programmable logic controllers, touch panels, and smart automation systems.

In industrial environments, a control device helps improve safety, accuracy, and efficiency. For example, it can regulate temperature, control motor speed, manage production lines, or activate emergency shutdown procedures. In homes, control devices are commonly used in heating systems, lighting, security systems, and smart appliances.

A well-designed control device should be reliable, easy to use, and responsive. It should provide clear feedback to the user and operate safely under different conditions. As technology continues to develop, modern control devices are becoming more intelligent, allowing remote access, automatic adjustments, and integration with digital networks.

Overall, a control device plays a key role in making systems easier to operate, safer to manage, and more efficient in everyday and professional applications.

counterfactuals.output: An object of the present invention is to appropriately control a wet/dry state of an electrolyte membrane of a fuel cell while suppressing deterioration of power generation stability and reduction in fuel utilization efficiency. A fuel cell system includes a fuel cell having an electrolyte membrane, a cathode gas supply system, an anode gas supply system, an anode off-gas circulation passage for returning anode off-gas discharged from an anode of the fuel cell to an anode inlet side, a circulation device configured to circulate the anode off-gas, and a control device. The control device acquires or estimates a wet/dry state parameter indicating a water content state of the electrolyte membrane, determines a target wet/dry state of the electrolyte membrane in accordance with an operating condition of the fuel cell, and controls a plurality of manipulated physical quantities capable of changing the wet/dry state of the electrolyte membrane. The plurality of manipulated physical quantities include, for example, at least one of a cathode gas flow rate, a cathode gas pressure, an anode gas pressure, a fuel cell temperature, a coolant flow rate, a generated current, a cathode stoichiometric ratio, and an anode gas circulation flow rate. The control device sets priority among the plurality of manipulated physical quantities in accordance with an operating region, a deviation between the wet/dry state parameter and the target wet/dry state, a responsiveness of each manipulated physical quantity, an influence on output performance, and/or an influence on fuel consumption, and preferentially changes a manipulated physical quantity having a higher priority so that the electrolyte membrane approaches the target wet/dry state. When the anode gas circulation flow rate is selected as one of the manipulated physical quantities, the control device executes a circulation flow rate limiting function for limiting an increase or decrease in the anode gas circulation flow rate on the basis of at least one of an anode pressure, a hydrogen concentration, a nitrogen concentration, a water vapor amount, a differential pressure across the electrolyte membrane, a required output, a purge state, and an allowable operating range of the circulation device. Accordingly, excessive circulation that may cause flooding, drying, pressure fluctuation, hydrogen dilution, noise, or electric power consumption is suppressed, and shortage of circulation that may cause local fuel starvation or uneven humidity distribution is also prevented. Thus, the wet/dry state of the electrolyte membrane can be controlled with high accuracy by coordinated control of a plurality of physical quantities while priority is dynamically assigned thereto, and the anode gas circulation flow rate is restricted within a suitable range, whereby both suppression of drying and suppression of flooding of the electrolyte membrane are achieved and durability, startability, response performance, and power generation efficiency of the fuel cell are improved.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe, in formal patent language, a control device of a fuel cell system that prevents rapid changes in anode gas circulation flow during transient membrane humidification control while compensating the control quantity using lower-priority manipulated parameters.
counterfactuals.output:
A control device for a fuel cell system is provided, the fuel cell system including a fuel cell stack having an anode and a cathode, an anode gas supply passage, an anode off-gas circulation passage, an anode gas circulation device configured to circulate anode off-gas to the anode, and a plurality of auxiliary devices for regulating an operating state of the fuel cell stack. The control device includes one or more processors configured to execute membrane humidification control for changing a target humidification state of an electrolyte membrane of the fuel cell stack during a transient operating condition.

In the control device, a plurality of manipulated parameters are assigned different control priorities for achieving a required control quantity relating to the membrane humidification control. The manipulated parameters include at least an anode gas circulation flow rate of the anode gas circulation device as a relatively high-priority manipulated parameter, and one or more lower-priority manipulated parameters including, for example, a cathode gas flow rate, a cathode gas pressure, a coolant temperature, an anode gas supply amount, an anode purge amount, or an electric power generation operating point of the fuel cell stack.

The control device is configured such that, when the membrane humidification control is performed during a transient state in which a requested output of the fuel cell stack changes, a variation rate or variation amount of the anode gas circulation flow rate is restricted so as to prevent a rapid change in the anode gas circulation flow. When a required change amount of the control quantity cannot be satisfied by the restricted change of the anode gas circulation flow rate, the control device compensates for an insufficient portion of the control quantity by changing at least one of the lower-priority manipulated parameters.

More specifically, the control device calculates a target control quantity for transient humidification control, determines a permitted change range of the anode gas circulation flow rate based on a predetermined rate limit, upper and lower guard values, or a transient protection condition, and sets a corrected target anode gas circulation flow rate within the permitted change range. The control device further calculates a deviation between the target control quantity and a control quantity achievable by the corrected target anode gas circulation flow rate, and distributes the deviation to the one or more lower-priority manipulated parameters. Accordingly, the control device suppresses abrupt fluctuation of hydrogen concentration, anode pressure, water transport, and gas distribution in the anode system while maintaining responsiveness of the membrane humidification control.

The lower-priority manipulated parameters may be selected in accordance with an operating condition of the fuel cell system, and a compensation amount assigned to each lower-priority manipulated parameter may be determined according to a priority order, a response characteristic, an allowable operating range, or an efficiency loss associated with the corresponding manipulated parameter. When the compensation by a first lower-priority manipulated parameter reaches a limit value, a remaining compensation amount may be assigned to a further lower-priority manipulated parameter.

By this configuration, even when transient humidification control requires an increase or decrease in a humidification-related control quantity, the anode gas circulation flow rate is not changed rapidly. Instead, the control device preserves stability of the anode circulation system and compensates the restricted portion of the control action using manipulated parameters having lower priority. As a result, membrane hydration can be appropriately controlled during transient operation while suppressing deterioration of fuel cell performance, hydrogen starvation, flooding, drying of the electrolyte membrane, and degradation of durability caused by rapid changes in anode gas circulation flow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
